user_input: What does Section 2 cover in the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997?
reference: Section 2 contains the definitions used in the Act, including terms such as armed forces, civil armed forces, court, explosives, firearms, terrorism, terrorist property, proscribed organization, and proscribed person.
response:
**Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997 – Section 2 (Definitions)**  

Section 2 is titled **“Definitions”** and sets out the meanings of a number of terms that are used elsewhere in the Act. The definitions provided in the retrieved excerpt are:

- **(a) “armed forces”** – the Military, Naval and Air Forces of Pakistan and the Reserves of such Forces. [Source 1]  
- **(b) “civil armed forces”** – the Frontier Constabulary, Frontier Corps, Pakistan Coast Guards, Pakistan Rangers or any other civil armed force notified by the Federal Government as such. [Source 1]  
- **(c) “Code”** – the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898). [Source 1]  
- **(d) “child”** – a person who at the time of the commission of the offence has not attained the age of eighteen years. [Source 1]  
- **(e) “court”** – an Anti‑terrorism Court established under section 13. [Source 1]  
- **(f) “explosives”** – any bomb, grenade, dynamite, or explosive substance capable of causing injury to any person or damage to any property and includes any explosive substance as defined in the Explosives Act, 1884 (Act IV of 1884). [Source 1]  
- **(g) “firearms”** – any or all types and gauges of handguns, rifles and shotguns, whether automatic, semi‑automatic or bolt‑action, and shall include all other firearms as defined in the Arms Ordinance, 1965 (W. P. Ord. XX. of 1965). [Source 1]  
- **(h) “fine”** – a pecuniary amount to be determined by the Court having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case. [Source 1]  
- **(ha) “freeze”** – to prohibit the transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of any money or other property. [Source 1]  
- **(i) “Government”** – the Federal Government or, as the case may be, a Provincial Government. [Source 1]  
- **(j) “grievous”** – in relation to bodily injury, any emasculation, mutilation, incapacitation, disfigurement or severe harm or hurt; and in relation to property, severe loss, damage or destruction. [Source 1]  
- **(k) “High Court”** – the High Court having territorial jurisdiction in respect of the area for which an Anti‑terrorism Court has been established. [Source 1]  
- **(l) “hijacking”** – any unlawful seizure or exercise of control, or any attempt at unlawful seizure or exercise of control, of an aircraft, by force, violence, threat or any form of obstruction, directly or through any other person, from within or outside the aircraft. [Source 1]  
- **(m) “hostage taking”** – the holding of a person captive with threats made to kill or harm that person if demands are not met. [Source 1]  
- **(n) “kidnapping for ransom”** – the action of conveying any person from any place, without his consent, or by force compelling or by any deceitful means inducing him, to go from any place, and unlawfully detaining him and demanding or attempting to demand money, pecuniary or other benefit from him or from another person, as a condition of his release. [Source 1]  
- **(o) “meeting”** – a meeting of two or more persons, whether in public or private. [Source 1]  
- **(oa) “money”** – includes coins or notes in any currency, postal orders, money orders, bank credits, bank accounts, letters of credit, travelers’ cheques, bank cheques, bankers’ drafts, in any form, electronic, digital or otherwise and such other kinds of monetary instruments or documents as the Federal Government may by order specify. [Source 1]  
- **(p) “organization”** – any group, combination or body of persons ****. [Source 1]  
- **(pa) “person”** – any natural, legal person or body corporate. [Source 1]  
- **(paa) “property”** – property of every description, whether corporeal or incorporeal, movable or immovable, tangible or intangible and includes shares, securities, bonds and deeds and instruments evidencing title to, or an interest in, property of any kind and money. [Source 1]  
- **(q) “proscribed organization”** – any organization which is listed in the First … (the excerpt ends before the full definition is given). [Source 1]  

These definitions collectively constitute the scope of Section 2, providing the interpretative framework for the rest of the Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997.

user_input: What does Section 7 cover in the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997?
reference: Section 7 sets out the punishments for acts of terrorism, with different penalties depending on whether death, hurt, grievous harm, grievous damage, kidnapping for ransom, hijacking, explosives, sectarian hate conduct, or another terrorist act is involved.
response:
**Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997 – Section 7  
“Punishment for acts of terrorism”**

Section 7 prescribes the penalties that apply to anyone who commits an act of terrorism as defined in Section 6.

1. **General framework** – The section applies to “whoever commits an act of terrorism under section 6” and sets out a series of sub‑clauses (a to i) that specify the punishment according to the nature and consequences of the terrorist act. [Source 1]

2. **Punishments for specific outcomes**  

   * **(a) Death caused** – If the act causes the death of any person, the offender is punishable, on conviction, with **death or imprisonment for life, and with fine**. [Source 1]  
   * **(b) Likely to cause death or endanger life (but no death or hurt caused)** – Punishable with **imprisonment of either description for a term not less than ten years but may extend to imprisonment for life, and with fine**. [Source 1]  
   * **(c) Grievous bodily harm or injury** – Punishable with **imprisonment of either description for a term not less than ten years but may extend to imprisonment for life, and also liable to a fine**. [Source 1]  
   * **(d) Grievous damage to property** – Punishable with **imprisonment of either description for a term not less than ten years (may extend to imprisonment for life), and also liable to a fine**. [Source 1]  
   * **(e) Kidnapping for ransom or hostage‑taking** – Punishable with **death or imprisonment for life**. [Source 1]  
   * **(f) Hijacking** – Punishable with **death or imprisonment for life and fine**. [Source 1]  

3. **Punishments for acts falling under particular sub‑clauses of Section 6(2)**  

   * **(ff)** – If the act falls under Section 6(2)(ee), the penalty is **imprisonment of not less than fourteen years but may extend to imprisonment for life**. [Source 1]  
   * **(g)** – If the act falls under Section 6(2)(f) and (g), the penalty is **imprisonment of not less than two years and not more than five years, and with fine**. [Source 1]  
   * **(h)** – If the act falls under clauses (h) to (n) of sub‑section 2 of Section 6, the penalty is **imprisonment of not less than five years (may extend to imprisonment for life) and with fine**. [Source 1]  

4. **Punishment for any other act of terrorism** – For acts not covered by clauses (a) to (h) and not covered by any other provision of the Act, the penalty is **imprisonment of not less than five years and not more than ten years, or with fine, or with both**. [Source 1]

5. **Additional consequence** – Clause (2) of Section 7 provides that an accused convicted of an offence under this Act shall be punishable with **imprisonment of ten years or more**; for the offences of kidnapping for ransom and hijacking, the convicted person **shall also be liable to forfeiture of property**. [Source 1]

**Summary** – Section 7 of the Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997 enumerates the range of punishments—ranging from death, life imprisonment, fixed‑term imprisonment (minimum ten years for the most serious outcomes, lower minima for certain categories), fines, and property forfeiture—applicable to various terrorist acts defined in Section 6. [Source 1]

user_input: What does Section 11B cover?
reference: Section 11B covers the proscription of organizations and allows the Federal Government to list an organization as proscribed in the First Schedule when the statutory grounds are met.
response:
**Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997 – Section 11B – “Proscription of organizations”**

**(1) Power to proscribe** – The Federal Government may, by an order published in the official Gazette, list an organization as a proscribed organization in the First Schedule on an ex parte basis, **if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the organization is**:  
  (a) concerned in terrorism;  
  (b) owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, by any individual or organization already proscribed under this Act; or  
  (c) acting on behalf of, or at the direction of, any individual or organization proscribed under this Act. [Source 1]

**Explanation** – The “reasonable grounds” opinion may be formed on the basis of information received from any credible source, whether domestic or foreign, including governmental and regulatory authorities, law‑enforcement agencies, financial intelligence units, banks and non‑banking companies, and international institutions. [Source 1]

**(2) Communication of grounds** – The grounds for proscription must be communicated to the proscribed organization within three days of the passing of the proscription order. [Source 1]

user_input: What does Section 11EE cover?
reference: Section 11EE covers the proscription of a person and the powers that may follow once a person is listed in the Fourth Schedule.
response:
**Section 11EE – “Proscription of person” (Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997)**  

The provision authorises the Federal Government to list a person in the Fourth Schedule as a *proscribed person* and sets out the grounds, procedures, powers, and penalties attached to such proscription.  

**(1) Grounds for proscription** – The Government may, by an order published in the official Gazette and on an ex‑parte basis, list a person if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the person is:  

* (a) concerned in terrorism;  
* (b) an activist, office‑bearer or associate of an organization kept under observation under section 11D or proscribed under section 11B; and  
* (c) in any way concerned or suspected to be concerned with such an organization or affiliated with any group or organization suspected of terrorism or sectarianism, or acting on behalf of or at the direction of any person or organization proscribed under this Act.  

The “reasonable grounds” may be formed on information from any credible domestic or foreign source, including governmental and regulatory authorities, law‑enforcement agencies, financial intelligence units, banks, non‑banking companies, and international institutions.  

(1A) The grounds must be communicated to the proscribed person within three days of the order. [Source 1]  

**(2) Powers and actions once a person is listed** – When a name appears in the Fourth Schedule, the Government may, without prejudice to any other action under this Act or any other law, exercise the following powers:  

* (a) Require the person to execute a bond with one or more sureties, satisfactory to the District Police Officer, for good behaviour and non‑involvement in terrorism for a period not exceeding three years. Failure to furnish the bond or sureties may result in detention until the bond is executed or sureties are provided. A minor may execute the bond through sureties only.  
* (b) Require prior permission from the officer in‑charge of the relevant police station before moving from the person’s permanent residence, and require the person to keep the officer informed of places to be visited and persons to be met.  
* (c) Impose movement restrictions, reporting requirements, and compliance directions, including:  
  * (i) Restrict movements to places specified in the order;  
  * (ii) Require the person to report at specified times, places and modes;  
  * (iii) Require compliance with all directions;  
  * (iv) Prohibit residence within areas specified in the order.  
* (v) Prohibit banks, financial institutions and other entities from providing loans, credit facilities or financial support to the proscribed person.  
* (vi) Cancel any existing arms licences; the arms must be deposited with the nearest police station or, failing that, will be confiscated, and the holder will be liable under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965. No new licence may be issued.  
* (d) Prohibit the person from visiting or being within the surroundings of specified places without written permission of the officer in‑charge, including:  
  * schools, colleges and institutions for persons under 21 years or women;  
  * theatres, cinemas, fairs, amusement parks, hotels, clubs, restaurants, tea shops and other public entertainment venues;  
  * airports, railway stations, bus stands, telephone exchanges, television and radio stations;  
  * public or private parks, gardens and playing fields;  
  * sites of public meetings, processions or festivals.  
* (e) Authorise police or any other government agency to check and probe the assets of the proscribed person and of immediate family members (parents, wives, children) to ascertain legitimacy of income and expenditure. No order under (d) or (e) may be operative for more than three years.  
* (f) Permit monitoring and surveillance of the person’s activities by police, any other government agency, or any designated authority. [Source 1]  

**(3) Review and appeal** – An aggrieved person may file a written review application with the Federal Government within thirty days of the proscription order, stating the grounds. The Government must hear the applicant and decide within ninety days on reasonable grounds. If the review application is refused, the person may appeal to the High Court within thirty days. [Source 1]  

**(4) Penalty for violation** – Any person who violates any direction or order of the Federal Government, or any term of the bond under sub‑section (2), is punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term that may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. [Source 1]  

**Power to arrest and detain suspected persons (11EEE)** – The Government, if satisfied that it is necessary to prevent a listed person from acting, may issue a written order to arrest and detain the person for a period specified in the order, which may be extended up to a total of twelve months. The provisions of Article 10 of the Constitution of Pakistan apply mutatis mutandis to such arrest and detention. [Source 1]  

**Preventive detention for inquiry (11EEEE)** – The Government (or, where section 4 is invoked, the armed forces or civil armed forces) may, for up to three months (extendable subject to Article 10), issue an order for preventive detention of any person concerned with an offence under this Act relating to security, defence, public order, target killing, kidnapping for ransom, extortion, bhatta, or maintenance of supplies/services, where sufficient grounds exist. The inquiry must be conducted by a police officer of at least Superintendent rank or by a Joint Interrogation Team (JIT) as notified by the Government, and the detainee must be produced before a court or magistrate within twenty‑four hours. [Source 1]  

**Additional penalty for contravention of sub‑section (1) order** – Any contravention of an order made under sub‑section (1) is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term that may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. [Source 1]  

*The above summary reflects the material contained in the retrieved excerpts of Section 11EE of the Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997. If any part of the provision was omitted from the excerpts, that portion is not included here.*

reference: Section 19 covers the procedure and powers of the Anti-terrorism Court.
response:
**Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 – Section 19 (“Judge”)**  
The provision defines the term “Judge”. It states that “Judge” includes every person officially designated as a Judge and any person empowered by law to give a definitive judgment in a civil or criminal proceeding, or a judgment that would become definitive if not appealed or if confirmed by another authority. The definition also covers members of a body of persons authorized by law to give such judgments. An illustration clarifies that a Magistrate who can sentence to fine or imprisonment (with or without appeal) is considered a Judge. [Source 1]

**Anti‑Money Laundering Act, 2010 – Section 19 (“Presumption as to records or property in certain cases”)**  
This section deals with evidentiary presumptions when a public‑record document is found in a person’s possession during a survey or search, or when records are received from abroad and authenticated as prescribed. The Court or investigating/prosecuting agency shall:  
(a) presume that the signature and any handwritten parts of the document are those of the person whose handwriting is alleged, and that any execution or attestation was done by the person named; and  
(b) admit the document as evidence even if it is not duly stamped, provided it is otherwise admissible. [Source 2]

**Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997 – Section 19 (“Procedure and Powers of Anti‑terrorism Court”)**  
Section 19 contains a series of sub‑sections governing the functioning of Anti‑terrorism Courts (ATCs) and related investigative procedures. The key points extracted from the retrieved excerpt are:

* **(1)** An investigating officer under the Act must be a police officer of at least Inspector rank, or, if a Joint Investigation Team (JIT) is formed, a Superintendent‑rank officer heads the JIT, which may include members from intelligence, armed forces, or civil armed forces. The JIT consists of five members, with a quorum of three; it may co‑opt additional persons from any federal or provincial institution. [Source 3]

* **(2)** Any default by a police‑station in‑charge, investigating officer, or any person required by law that delays investigation or the submission of the report under sub‑section (1) is deemed wilful disobedience of the ATC’s orders and is punishable as contempt of court. [Source 3]

* **(3)** The ATC may take direct cognizance of a case triable by it without the case being sent under section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [Source 3]

* **(5)** When an accused released from police or other investigative custody is still under investigation, the ATC may, on good grounds shown by the public prosecutor or a law officer and with reasons recorded in writing, order the accused to be placed back in police or investigative custody for further investigation. [Source 3]

* **(6)** An Anti‑terrorism Court is deemed to be a Magistrate for the purpose of sub‑section (5). [Source 3]

* **(7)** After taking cognizance, the ATC must conduct the trial day‑to‑day and decide the case within seven days; failure to do so must be reported to the Chief Justice of the relevant High Court for appropriate directions. [Source 3]

* **(8)** The ATC may grant no more than two adjournments during the trial, and may impose exemplary costs. If defence counsel fails to appear after two consecutive adjournments, the Court may appoint a State Counsel (with at least seven years’ standing in criminal matters) from its panel of advocates, in consultation with the Government, to represent the accused. [Source 3]

* **(8a)** Non‑compliance with the provisions of sub‑sections (7) or (8) may subject the presiding officer to disciplinary action by the concerned High Court. [Source 3]

* **(8b)** If consent or sanction of the appropriate authority is not obtained within thirty days of a challan’s submission, such consent is deemed given, and the Court may proceed with the trial. [Source 3]

* **(9)** A change in the composition of the ATC or transfer of a case does not require the Court to recall and rehear witnesses; it may act on the evidence already recorded. [Source 3]

* **(10)** An accused may be tried in his absence if the Court, after an inquiry, is satisfied that the absence is deliberate and intended to impede justice. This requires a published proclamation in at least one daily newspaper (including Sindhi) giving the accused seven days to appear, failing which action may be taken under section 88 of the Code. The Court must then appoint a State‑funded advocate to defend the absent accused. [Source 3]

* **(11)** The advocate appointed under sub‑section (10) is selected by the ATC and engaged at Government expense. [Source 3]

* **(11A)** The provisions of sub‑sections (10) and (11) do not deny the accused the right to consult or be defended by a lawyer of his own choice. [Source 3]

* **(12)** If, within sixty days of conviction, a person tried under sub‑section (10) appears voluntarily or is apprehended and proves that he did not abscond, the ATC shall set aside the conviction and retry him. The Court may also exercise this power after the sixty‑day period if the person shows that circumstances beyond his control prevented earlier appearance. [Source 3]

* **(14)** Subject to other provisions of the Act, an Anti‑terrorism Court has all the powers of a Court of Sessions for trial purposes and shall try offences as if it were a Court of Sessions, following the procedure prescribed in the Code of Criminal Procedure. [Source 3]

*Additional procedural details* (not numbered in the excerpt) specify that the investigating officer must complete the investigation within thirty working days, forward a report under section 173 of the Code through the public prosecutor, and, if the investigation exceeds thirty days, submit an interim report within three days after the period expires, allowing the Court to commence trial on that basis. [Source 3]

*The excerpt also contains provisions (1A) and (1B) allowing the Federal Government to transfer investigations to other agencies and directing the hand‑over of persons arrested by armed forces to the police investigating officer. [Source 3]

These sub‑sections together define the scope, powers, procedural timelines, and safeguards associated with the functioning of Anti‑terrorism Courts under the Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997. [Source 3]

reference: Section 11EEEEE(2) says that contravention of an order made under subsection (1) is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term that may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
response:
Under the **Anti‑Terrorism Act, 1997**, Section 11EE (“Proscription of person”) provides that:

- **Section 11EE(2)**: Any person who contravenes an order made under sub‑section (1) (i.e., a preventive‑disposal order issued during an inquiry or investigation) is liable, on conviction, to **rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years**, **or to a fine**, **or to both**.
